job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Zoe Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake up at 8, which is a luxury, because I work at Kestrel Digital, a small marketing agency in Brindle, and we start at 9:30. I'm on the campaigns team as a junior account coordinator, so I schedule posts, pull reports and write the first draft of client updates. I do a lot of that with AI tools, honestly all day. I rent a box room above a vape shop with two other people, and my student loan is about 36,000. Evenings I do small freelance jobs, like fixing a local bakery's spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, that's a relief, and also a bit boring. At work I'd tell Marcus, my boss, that we should keep using the tools for the routine stuff and spend the saved time on ideas. Online I'd post that the hype was loud but the useful bits are still useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be okay but not rich. My job's safe, my pay's 22,800, and the loan plus rent eat most of it. I'd be restless, because a slow world isn't the one I'm preparing for. I'd feel like I'd learned all this for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and use the time to build my freelance work. I'd aim for two regular clients by spring, maybe 300 a month extra, and put it all against the loan. I'd also apply for an account executive job at a bigger agency in the city in about a year, since Brindle has so few openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly deflated. I'm someone who likes things moving, so a flat future feels like waiting for a bus. But the bills are the actual pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the city, if nothing is changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Brindle only has three agencies, and Marcus can't promote me past coordinator. If I want pay to go up, I need more options. It's more about the town than about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the freelance work didn't take off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd drop the plan for a year and do overtime at Kestrel. It's not a disaster, it just means the loan lasts longer. I'd probably sell the camera I bought for content work, which stings.

I'd tell Marcus (my boss) to spend saved time on **ideas**.

Apply for an account executive job in the **city** in about a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment where people split into those who use the tools and those who get used. I'd tell Marcus we should reorganise around it, and post online about how to build skills in public. I'd also say we need rules, because a lot of this could go unfair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the coordinator job shrinks fast. Scheduling, drafting, reports, I do those with AI already, and a client could do them too. But I might be good at the next layer, strategy and keeping clients happy. I'm worried, but I also feel a bit ahead of most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Marcus a new role for myself that covers tool setup and quality checks for clients. I'd start a small paid newsletter about AI tools for local shops, to make my name. I'd learn the tools properly through two weekend courses, and I'd keep freelancing. Also I'd join a graduates' campaign for a minimum pay for juniors, since I think rules matter too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix of excited and nervous. I like the pace. But I also know I'm one of the people the change is aimed at, so I can't pretend it's all good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you feel ahead of most people. What if everyone else catches up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They will, within a year or two, and I know that. So being ahead of the crowd with the tools isn't a plan, it's a head start. The plan is to be good with clients and numbers on top of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Kestrel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dee, the production assistant. She's 29, a single mum, and she doesn't like the tools. If Marcus has to cut, she's first. I'd offer to teach her on my lunch breaks, but I can't promise it'd save her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is crazy, and that anyone calling it manageable is selling something. I'd say we need emergency support, like a basic income and public ownership of the big systems. And I'd say it loudly, because I think people need to hear it from someone who actually uses the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my whole career goes. Marketing, finance, anything with a screen. I'm quick, but I'd be competing with something that never sleeps and costs nothing. I've got 36,000 of debt, under a month saved, and nobody to lean on, so a bad year ends the whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the next year. I'd get as much freelance as possible and sell my camera. I'd take a practical course for something hands-on, like electrical installation, since robots arrive later. I'd also join every group pushing for basic income and ask my landlord about a cheaper room. And I'd stay at Kestrel until they let me go, to keep the references.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty scared. It's the kind of fear where I try to be funny about it. But at night I'd just be refreshing my balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An electrician is quite a jump from marketing. Is that serious?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's serious as a backup. I'd rather have a trade with three extra years of safety than stay precious about the degree. I like fixing things, and my uncle Cem could take me on at weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your flatmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we should figure out the rent as a team before one of us gets laid off, and maybe get a smaller place together. I'd rather have a plan made when it's calm than a fight made when it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a chance if we move now. I'd write about it, speak about it, and tell my team to build skills that aren't just tool use. I'd push for a public fund that pays people to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm anxious but fairly well placed. I'm young and quick, and by 2031 I could be a senior in a niche that machines struggle with, like persuading clients in person. Or I could be out of that field entirely. Either way, I'd want money and skills ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run two tracks. Track one is in marketing: aim for an account executive job in the city within a year and learn the newest tools on the side. Track two is a small business of my own, maybe training local shops to use AI. I'd pay the loan down by 150 a month, because debt shrinks your options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised and a bit scared. It feels like being at the start of a race where nobody's sure of the finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the small business actually sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Setup and training, like an afternoon at a bakery showing them how to handle their orders and posts with AI. It's small money, maybe 80 a session, but it's my own and it teaches me what ordinary people struggle with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do if the city job doesn't come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I stay at Kestrel, push the side work and keep the loan payments going. I wouldn't count it as a failure. I'd count it as information about what to do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say it's enough time to build something good. I'd tell people to learn broadly, not just one tool, and to pressure governments for training and a share of the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pretty good. By 32 I could have cleared the loan and be doing something I chose, maybe my own small firm. I'd still worry for people who don't have the habit of learning, like Dee. But for me, a decade is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Kestrel for two more years, then move to a city agency or a tech start-up that wants someone who knows both marketing and the tools. I'd build the training side business properly, with a few clients on retainer. I'd clear the loan by about 28 and then save for a deposit. I'd also take some evening classes in statistics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm and curious. The nervous bit is small. Mostly I'd feel lucky to be young at the right time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the people who aren't good with change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I can't wave away. I'd try to teach those I know, like Dee, but I can't carry everyone. I'd want the government to run training that doesn't treat people as slow just because they're nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years change how you think about starting a family or buying a home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd think about a home by 30 and kids a few years later, if the work picture is clear. With two years I wouldn't even consider it. With ten, I can plan like a normal person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years doesn't give me the time to pay the loan, and I'm young with nobody to fall back on. What would help is a real basic income, fast, and training that pays you while you do it, not afterwards.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being good with AI doesn't make me safe. People assume the ones who use AI every day are fine, and I'm the one who can see how quickly it's getting better.

headlineQuote: People assume the ones who use AI every day are fine, and I'm the one who can see how quickly it's getting better.
portrait: **Zoe** is 22, a business graduate and junior account coordinator at a small agency in Brindle.
She uses **AI** tools all day, freelances in the evenings and owes about 36,000 with almost no savings.
She leans left, wants a **basic income** and public retraining, and also acts on her own fast.
She moves toward a **hands-on** trade as a backup in the two-year picture, but feels calm with a decade.
Her main limit is **Brindle**, a town with few agencies, as much as AI.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because two years is not enough to clear the loan and she has nobody to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A real **basic income**, quickly, and paid training that she can take while she works.
